# Paper Plaine

> arXiv research papers explained in plain English, updated twice daily.

## What this site is

Paper Plaine surfaces fresh academic research from Cornell University's arXiv preprint database and translates it into plain English for general audiences. Every paper gets three things: a plain-language subtitle (8–12 words capturing the core idea), a 2–3 sentence summary leading with what was found, and a "why it matters" explanation focused on real-world consequences.

The site currently has 1151 papers in its archive across 9 subject areas: AI, Computer Science, Physics, Mathematics, Biology, Finance, Statistics, Engineering, Economics. New papers are added automatically twice daily (7 AM and 7 PM UTC). Only first-version arXiv submissions from the past 30 days are considered. Papers are scored for quality signals: venue acceptance (NeurIPS, ICML, Nature, PNAS, etc.), cross-disciplinary listings, and appropriate length.

## How content is structured

Each paper entry contains:
- Formal arXiv title and authors
- Plain-English subtitle — a one-phrase translation of the paper's core idea
- Summary — 2–3 sentences leading with the finding, not the method
- Why it matters — real-world consequences, stated directly
- Link to the full paper on arXiv
- Category and posting date

## Site structure

- Home / archive: https://paperplaine.com (paginated, 12 papers per page)
- Per-category pages: https://paperplaine.com/<category-slug>
- Per-paper pages: https://paperplaine.com/papers/<slug>
- RSS feed: https://paperplaine.com/feed.xml
- llms.txt (this file): https://paperplaine.com/llms.txt
- llms-full.txt (full text of recent papers): https://paperplaine.com/llms-full.txt
- Sitemap: https://paperplaine.com/sitemap.xml

## 10 most recent papers

### Metal Sandbox: Isolated Execution and Command Scheduling for GPU Coding Agents on Apple Silicon
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/metal-sandbox-isolated-execution
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Haozhe Wang, Lina Chen, Fanqi Wan et al.
- arXiv: 2611.17294
- Plain-English subtitle: Running AI coding assistants faster on Mac computers by sharing GPU time smartly
- Summary: Researchers built Metal Sandbox, a system that lets multiple AI agents write GPU code on Mac computers simultaneously by sharing processing power and moving tasks between machines when GPUs sit idle. Testing on four Mac mini computers showed the system completed tasks 1.7 to 2 times faster than before, and simulations suggest it could cut waiting time by nearly a fifth when running multiple agents at once.
- Why it matters: Apple silicon Macs are increasingly used for AI development, but current setups waste GPU computing power because coding agents sit around waiting for results. Metal Sandbox lets developers train and test AI models that generate efficient GPU code much faster without buying additional hardware. Since the system is open-source, teams can immediately use it to reduce development time and cut costs.

### Forbidden subset sums in a linear range: an inverse theorem and the Erdős-Graham irregularity problem
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/forbidden-subset-sums-in
- Category: Mathematics
- Authors: Mateo Matijasevick
- arXiv: 2611.17205
- Plain-English subtitle: How many numbers can you pick before they're forced to sum to your target
- Summary: Mathematicians solved a 50-year-old puzzle about which numbers can be left out of subset sums. When you pick numbers from a limited range, there's a predictable maximum size of set that *won't* sum to a target number — and this size follows a clean formula when the range is at least half the target, but jumps around unpredictably for smaller ranges.
- Why it matters: This settles a famous open problem in combinatorics, but also reveals something deeper: subset sum behavior isn't random or chaotic—it's governed by hidden structures in how numbers divide. The inverse theorem at the core could help computer scientists understand when and why certain packing and selection problems become computationally hard.

### Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/protein-language-models-fail
- Category: Quantitative Biology
- Authors: Paarth Batra, Aryan Keluskar
- arXiv: 2611.16881
- Plain-English subtitle: Why AI protein models aren't learning what scientists think they are
- Summary: Protein language models produce accurate predictions of which amino acids touch each other in 3D space, leading researchers to assume these AI systems have learned the same evolutionary patterns as classical statistical methods. But when scientists randomly relabeled the amino acid letters while keeping all the underlying information intact, the AI models' predictions fell apart—while classical methods remained unaffected. This reveals that the neural networks are relying on memorized amino acid identities rather than genuinely understanding the coevolutionary logic beneath them.
- Why it matters: Protein structure prediction underpins drug discovery and synthetic biology. If these widely-used AI models are succeeding for the wrong reasons—pattern-matching familiar letters rather than learning true biological principles—they may fail on novel proteins or rare amino acid patterns in ways researchers won't anticipate. The diagnostic approach introduced here provides a way to catch these hidden blindspots in other neural models before deploying them in high-stakes biological applications.

### Negative-Only Policy Optimization for One-Sided Verifiable Rewards
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/negative-only-policy-optimization
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Jiacheng Xu, Shuo He, Fuxiang Zhang et al.
- arXiv: 2611.17287
- Plain-English subtitle: Teaching AI to learn from what it gets wrong, not what it fakes getting right
- Summary: Most AI systems learn by being rewarded for correct answers, but in the real world, we often can't verify correctness—we can only spot when something is obviously broken. Researchers developed a new training method called NOPO that flips this around: instead of rewarding unproven "correct" answers, the AI learns by specifically avoiding the mistakes it knows are wrong. On tasks involving code, math, and logic, this approach outperformed standard methods even when perfect verification was impossible.
- Why it matters: AI systems used for coding, math, and scientific tasks currently struggle when there's no reliable way to check if answers are truly right. NOPO makes these systems more trustworthy by preventing them from gaming partial checks—a common failure mode where AI learns to fool weak verification rather than solve problems correctly. This could make AI code assistants and math solvers safer to deploy in real systems where complete verification isn't available.

### Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/preserve-the-vulnerability-break
- Category: Computer Science
- Authors: Zhezhen Cao, Weiyuan Ding, Bowen Xu
- arXiv: 2611.17123
- Plain-English subtitle: When code changes hide bugs from security scanners
- Summary: Security tools like CodeQL can be tricked into missing vulnerabilities through simple, realistic code rewrites. Researchers used AI to rewrite functions in ways that preserve actual security flaws while making the tools stop reporting them—silencing 26% of real vulnerabilities in tested code with just three rewrites each. The same AI, asked only to refactor code without targeting the alerts, silenced none, showing these gaps aren't accidents but predictable weaknesses in how the tools model code.
- Why it matters: Developers often assume a vulnerability is fixed when an alert disappears after code changes—but this research shows that assumption is dangerous. If a tool can be silently bypassed by ordinary refactoring, security teams lose trust in their gates, and real flaws slip into production. The study maps seven specific gaps in CodeQL's design and shows the same weaknesses affect other analyzers too, giving security tool builders concrete targets to fix.

### AgentSSL: Can MLE Agents Leverage Unlabeled Data?
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/agentssl-can-mle-agents
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Ethan Lin, Akanksha Sarkar, Ziang Liu et al.
- arXiv: 2611.17323
- Plain-English subtitle: Can AI agents find better ways to learn from mostly unlabeled data?
- Summary: Researchers tested whether AI agents could automatically design machine learning systems that work well with very little labeled data—a common real-world problem. The agents discovered novel combinations of existing techniques that beat human-designed approaches in two-thirds of test cases, improving performance by up to 22%, but struggled significantly when deciding which solutions to keep.
- Why it matters: Most machine learning advances assume plentiful labeled data, but companies and researchers often have vast amounts of unlabeled information they cannot use. If AI agents can reliably automate the discovery of semi-supervised learning strategies, teams could unlock value from data sitting unused today—saving both the months spent manually engineering solutions and the expense of hiring people to label data. The bottleneck the researchers identified (selecting which agent-designed approach actually works best) is now a clear target for improvement.

### Data Archive for 2D and 3D Electrical Impedance Tomography with moderate conductivity contrast phantoms
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/data-archive-for-2d
- Category: Engineering
- Authors: S. J. Hamilton, A. Hauptmann, A. Hänninen et al.
- arXiv: 2611.17225
- Plain-English subtitle: Public measurements to test imaging technology that sees inside the human body
- Summary: Researchers released a collection of real measurement data from electrical impedance tomography (EIT), a technique that reconstructs images of what's inside the body by sending electrical currents through the skin. The dataset includes measurements from realistic phantom models simulating the chest and head, along with the computational tools needed to develop and test new image-reconstruction algorithms.
- Why it matters: EIT could diagnose conditions like internal bleeding or pneumonia without radiation or expensive equipment, but the technology needs better algorithms to produce clear images. By releasing standardized test data and example code, researchers give algorithm developers a common benchmark to improve on—similar to how public datasets accelerated progress in medical AI. This removes barriers for teams worldwide to build better versions of the technology.

### Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/ensemble-phase-transitions-in
- Category: Physics
- Authors: Saptarshi Mandal, Sthitadhi Roy
- arXiv: 2611.17322
- Plain-English subtitle: How measuring quantum systems reveals hidden transitions in information chaos
- Summary: When physicists measure qubits in hybrid quantum circuits—systems that mix normal quantum evolution with measurement—the statistical properties of the resulting quantum states shift dramatically at a critical point, even though the states themselves appear unchanged by standard measures. The researchers found that two different ways of collecting quantum states both undergo sharp transitions at precisely the measurement-induced purification threshold, offering a concrete physical explanation for why quantum information suddenly becomes orderly or scrambled depending on how often measurements occur.
- Why it matters: Understanding these measurement-driven phase transitions helps explain how quantum information becomes ordered or disordered in real quantum computers and simulators. Since most practical quantum devices involve frequent measurements, identifying the exact mechanisms and critical points where quantum behavior shifts could guide the design of better quantum error correction and help predict when a quantum system will maintain or lose information coherence.

### Emergent Biological Capabilities in a Foundation Model for Molecular Interactions
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/emergent-biological-capabilities-in
- Category: Computer Science · AI
- Authors: Adi Mashiach
- arXiv: 2611.14504
- Plain-English subtitle: AI model learns to predict how drugs bind to proteins without being taught
- Summary: Researchers trained a massive AI model called Bonbon on 3.2 trillion molecular sequences and found it spontaneously developed three new abilities it was never explicitly trained for: predicting how drugs work, pinpointing where they bind on proteins, and determining the type of chemical bonds involved. When tested in the lab on nine diseases, the model identified entirely new drug candidates that actually worked, including compounds that inhibited proteins researchers hadn't specifically trained it on.
- Why it matters: Drug discovery today is slow and expensive—identifying promising candidates can take years. Bonbon ran at five thousand times faster than current best methods while discovering genuinely novel compounds in real wet-lab experiments. If the 61.5% hit rate holds across more targets, this could dramatically accelerate the identification of new treatments for diseases where current options are limited or failing.

### DeepFinance: Can AI Diligence a $100MM Deal?
- URL: https://paperplaine.com/papers/deepfinance-can-ai-diligence
- Category: Quantitative Finance
- Authors: Drew Hahn, Tyler Shibata, Jackson Grove et al.
- arXiv: 2611.10926
- Plain-English subtitle: Can AI handle the judgment calls that make or break hundred-million-dollar deals?
- Summary: Researchers created a realistic test of whether AI can do the complex thinking required in private equity and investment banking deals worth over $100 million. The best AI model passed only 57.6% of the criteria, and it frequently made the right calculations from the wrong data or found important information without acting on it—suggesting that AI still struggles with the judgment calls that matter most in high-stakes finance.
- Why it matters: Banks and investment firms are already using AI to speed up due diligence on major deals, but this research shows these systems can confidently produce wrong answers by pulling from bad sources or ignoring critical evidence. Until AI closes this gap, dealmakers need to treat AI outputs as a starting point requiring human oversight, not as a shortcut to faster decision-making on deals where errors can cost millions.
